title: Relative cult is exactly what the precept forbids—no sane painter treats the panel as absolute God
source_text: XXVI. Quam vanum sit autem istud effugium, inde manifestum est, quod sensus communis dictat, eum qui pingit, vel fingit imaginem aliquam Dei qui in coelis est, aut aliarum quae sunt in eis potestatum, eique imagini aliquem cultum & honorem religiose defert, id eo animo facere, ut per illam Deum honoret, & alia ad quorum similitudinem facta est; ac proinde honorem qui in isto casu imagini defertur, ad alium referri, & sic non absolutum, sed relativum esse. At hoc ipsum est praecise quod Deus hoc praecepto vetat; non vero solum ne quis imaginem Dei faciat, eique cultum exhibeat, non propter Deum quem illa exprimi existimat, sed tantum propter ipsam, quam habeat pro summo Deo, qui illa exprimitur: quod ita absurdum est & contradictorium, ut cadere non possit in eum, qui saltem adhuc aliquo modo ratione utitur. Quo modo enim ille ipse, qui Dei imaginem in tabula pingi curat, in animum suum inducere poterit, tabellam illam esse ipsum Deum, quem in ea voluit esse repraesentatum, eique tabellae deberi summum religionis cultum, non propter numen cujus imago est, sed propter ipsam quam scit meris coloribus & lineis constare? Quae insomnia tam rara est atque inusitata, ut non opus fuerit illam singulari interdicto in lege cohiberi.
pass_a_gloss: But how vain that escape is, is thence made plain, that common sense dictates that he who paints, or fashions, some image of God who is in the heavens, or of other powers which are in them, and religiously pays to that image some cult and honor, does that with this mind, that through it he may honor God, and the others to whose likeness it was made; and accordingly that the honor which in that case is paid to the image is referred to another, and so is not absolute, but relative. But this itself is precisely what God forbids by this commandment; not indeed only that no one make an image of God, and exhibit cult to it, not on account of God whom he thinks it expresses, but only on account of itself, which he would hold for the highest God, who is expressed by it: which is so absurd and contradictory, that it cannot fall upon him who at least still uses reason in some mode. For how could that very man, who causes an image of God to be painted on a panel, bring it into his mind that that little tablet is God himself, whom he wished to be represented in it, and that the highest cult of religion is due to that tablet, not on account of the divinity whose image it is, but on account of itself which he knows to consist of mere colors and lines? Which madness is so rare and unusual, that there was no need for it to be restrained by a singular interdict in the law.
pass_b_english: Everyday sense: anyone who paints God and bows to the panel means relative honor through it—not absolute godhood of paint.
The precept targets precisely that relative move; absolute tablet-worship is too absurd to need its own ban.

choices.why: Rome’s narrowed reading of the precept.
